# Forwards and futures. 

## Problem #1 (25 points)
### The Dow index and Dow futures
Please, in no particular order read the Wikipedia entry about *futures contracts* and listen to the fun and educational episode of *Planet money* about credit risk in cafeteria futures. Both are linked below:

[Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Futures_contract): Futures

[Planet money](https://www.npr.org/sections/money/2016/01/06/462149561/episode-15-delicious-cake-futures): Delicious cake futures

**(10 points)** Provide the definitions of the forward contract and the futures contract. Then, highlight at least two similarities and at least two differences between the two. 
Forward Contract: A customized, private over-the-counter (OTC) agreement between two parties to buy or sell an underlying asset at a specified future date at a predetermined price agreed upon today. Because they are private contracts, they carry counterparty credit risk (as  illustrated in the Planet Money cafeteria futures episode regarding delivery and default risk).

**Futures Contract:** A standardized, legally binding agreement to buy or sell a predetermined quantity of an underlying asset at a specified price on a specific future delivery date. Futures are traded on organized exchanges and backed by a central clearinghouse, which eliminates counterparty risk through daily mark-to-market settlements and margin accounts.

**Similarities:** They are both similar in the obligation aspect. Both are derivative contracts that obligate the buyer to purchase (and the seller to deliver/sell) the underlying asset at a future date at a fixed price.

They are also both primarily utilized by market participants for hedging existing price risks or for speculation.

**Differences:** Their Market Structure is different. Forward contracts are completely customized and traded over-the-counter (OTC) between private parties, whereas futures contracts are highly standardized in terms of contract size, expiration dates, and delivery specifications, and are traded on public exchanges.

Their Counterparty Risk & Settlement is also different. For example, forward contracts carry direct counterparty credit risk (if the counterparty defaults at maturity). On the other hand, futures contracts eliminate individual counterparty risk because the exchange's clearinghouse acts as the intermediary, utilizing daily mark-to-market (daily settlement of gains and losses) and margin requirements.

The files "dow.csv" and "dow-futures.csv" contain index prices and the futures prices for delivery on a particular date in the future. 


**(5 points)**
Import the data into a data frame (or two?). Draw the time-plot of the evolution of the closing index prices and the futures prices on the same coordinate system. You do **not** need to put the calendar days on the horizontal axis, but you **do** need to label your axes and give your time-plot a title indicating the dates. Make sure that you plot the two trajectories in **different** colors indicating in the text which color corresponds to which company. 

Here is a link to a straightforward tutorial which will help you accomplish the above neatly: 

[Timeline plotting](https://statisticsglobe.com/draw-multiple-time-series-in-same-plot-in-r) 

```{r}
library(readr)
dow <- read_csv("/Users/sammarino/Downloads/dow.csv")
dow.futures <- read_csv("/Users/sammarino/Downloads/dow-futures.csv")
dow$Date<-as.Date(dow$Date)
dow.futures$Date <- as.Date(dow.futures$Date)
plot(dow$Date,dow$Close, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "peru", xlab = "Date", ylab = "Price", main = "Dow Jones Index vs. Dow Futures Prices\n(May 9, 2022 – February 14, 2023)")
lines(dow.futures$Date,dow.futures$Close, type = "l", col = "blue", lwd = 2)
legend("bottomleft", legend = c("Dow Index (Spot) - Burnt Orange", "Dow Futures - Blue"), col = c("peru", "blue"), lwd = 2)
```

**(10 points)**
What do you notice when you compare the timeplots? Which of the **formulae** for calculating futures prices you encountered on the Wikipedia entry come in handy?

We noticed a few things when looking at the timeplots. Firstly we can see
high Correlation / tracking between the two lines. The two curves move almost identically in tandem throughout the entire time horizon (May 2022 to February 2023), reflecting strong co-movement in response to macroeconomic news and market conditions.

Another thing we can see is the Basis/Spread: The futures price trajectory generally stays very close to the spot index price, exhibiting a slight premium or discount (the basis) depending on prevailing interest rates and dividend yields over the life of the contract.

The primary formula from the Wikipedia entry on futures contracts that explains this relationship is the Cost-of-Carry Model (or the forward/futures pricing formula for stock indices):$$F_0 = S_0 e^{(r - q)T}$$
Where: $F_0$ is the futures price today.
$S_0$ is the spot price of the underlying index (dow.csv).
$r$ is the risk-free interest rate.
$q$ is the continuous dividend yield of the index constituents.
$T$ is the time to maturity of the futures contract.
This formula explains why futures and spot prices track each other so closely, as any persistent divergence beyond the cost of carry (interest costs minus dividend earnings) would trigger arbitrage opportunities (cash-and-carry or reverse cash-and-carry trades), pulling the prices back into theoretical alignment.


# Call price properties
## Problem #2 (25 points)
### Apple calls
The file "apple-calls.csv" contains call prices observed on February 14th for European call options on the stocks of Apple Inc with expiry on May 19th and with varying strike prices. 

**(5 points)**
Import the data into a data frame. Create a line plot of the mid price (defined as the midpoint between the bid and the ask price) as it depends on the strike. 
```{r}
appd = read.csv("apple-calls.csv")
midprice = (appd$Bid + appd$Ask) / 2
appd[12] = midprice
plot(type = "l", x = appd$Strike, y = midprice, xlab = "Strike", ylab = "Mid Price", lwd = 2, main = "Mid Price vs Strike of AAPL")

```


**(5 points)**
What do you notice about the monotonicity and convexity of the above curve? 

The curve is strictly monotonically decreasing and convex.

**(15 points)**
**Prove** that the same conclusions regarding the monotonicity and convexity of the call prices with respect to the strike must hold in general **under the no arbitrage assumption**. 

Let C(K) be the call price for a strike K call option.

1. Prove C(K) Decreasing with K

Suppose $K_1$ < $K_2$. Then, for every value of S(T), S(T) - $K_1$ ≥ S(T) - $K_2$
Now assume to the contrary that C($K_1$) < C($K_2$). 
Then, you can buy the $K_1$ call and sell the $K_2$ call, so your time 0 cash flow will be C($K_2$) - C$K_1$) > 0, a net inflow
On the exercise date, the payoff is $(S(T) - K_1)_+ - (S(T) - K_2)_+$ which is positive in every state of the world. 
This is an arbitrage!
Therefore, $C(K_1) ≥ C(K_2)$, but in practice, S(T) typically has a positive probability of being greater than the strike price making the monotonicity strict.

2. Prove convexity of C(K) with K

Suppose $K_1 < K_2 < K_3$ such that $K_2 =𝝀K_1 + (1-𝝀)K_3$ 
which gives you 𝝀= $(K_3-K_2) / (K_3-K_1)$ where 0 < 𝝀 < 1
Now assume a portfolio that longs 𝝀 calls at $K_1$, (1-𝝀) calls at $K_3$, and shorts 1 call at $K_2$
The payoff = $λ(S(T) − K_1)_+ + (1−λ)(S(T) − K_3)_+ − (S(T) − K_2)_+$

Unpacking each region:
If $S(T) < K_1$, payoff = 0
If $K_1 < S(T) < K_2$ then payoff = $λ(S(T) - K_1)$
If $K_2 < S(T) < K_3$ then payoff = $λ(S(T) - K_1) - (S(T)-K_2) = (1-λ)(K_3 - S(T)) ≥ 0$ 
Finally, If $S(T) > K_3$ then payoff $K_2 − λK_1 − (1−λ)K_3$ = 0

Since payoff ≥ 0 in every state, the portfolio's cost must also be ≥ 0 to meet the no-arbitrage condition.

Therefore, $λC(K_1) + (1−λ)C(K_3) − C(K_2)$ ≥ 0
which is the definition of convex.

# Put-call parity

## Problem #3 (25 points)
**(5 points)**
Using put-call parity, find the formula for the interest rate if all other ingredients are known. 

$V_C(0) - V_P(0) = S_o - Ke^{-rt}$
$-(V_C(0) - V_P(0) - S_o)/K= e^{-rt}$
$\frac{ln((k)/(-(V_C(0) - V_P(0) - S_o))}{t} = r$



**(5 points)** 
Based on the above, what can you say about the interest rates $r$ you expect to obtain for varying values of the strike price? Bear in mind the **standing assumptions** we made in the beginning of the semester. 

Keeping with the standing assumptions, $r$ is directly related to the market and its value is not determined or changed given a specific strike price. If all else stays the same, an increasing strike price will lead to a lower value of $r$ and vise versa, although their values are not inherently based on causation. 

**(10 points)**
Based on the data set "apple-parity.csv", calculate the continuously compounded, risk-free interest rate for all the strike prices given. Be careful about how you use the *bid* and *ask/offer* prices of the options. Set $T=0.25$. Plot the values of the interest rate you obtain as they depend on the strike prices. 


```{r}
apple_parity <- read.csv("apple-parity.csv")
t=.25
s_o <- apple_parity$Stock
k <- apple_parity$Strike

#r = ln(k/(-Vc(0) + Vp(0) + s_o)/t

r1 <- log(k/(-apple_parity$BidCall + apple_parity$AskPut + s_o))/t
r2 <- log(k/(-apple_parity$AskCall + apple_parity$BidPut + s_o))/t


plot(k, r2, pch = 16, type = "b", col = "red",
     xlab = "Strike Price (k)", 
     ylab = "Implied Interest Rate (r)",
     main = "Apple Interest Rates Associated to Strike Prices")
lines(k, r1, type = "b", pch = 16, col = "blue")

legend("bottomleft", pch = 16, lty = 1, col = c("red", "blue"),
       legend = c("interest rate (high)", "interest rate (low)"))

```


**(5 points)**
What do you notice about the above plot? Does it or does it not agree with your prediction from the second question in the problem? Substantiate your answer. 

The plot above does not agree with our prediction entirely. Since we determined that $r$ is a market related variable and not dependent upon strike price (they are simply correlated but do not have a causal relationship), in theory $r$ should be a relatively consistent value. Looking at the above plot, $r$ is relatively constant for strike prices until we get to about $k = 160$ in which the interest rate makes a significant drop in value. Looking at the high interest rate where we will sell the call and buy the put, the interest rate for low strike prices hover at around 3.5%-4% before dropping below 2.5% as the strike price increases. The low interest rate follows a similar pattern with constant $r$ hovering around 2.7%-3.5% until we get to higher strike prices where it drops to 2% and below.
